newsitem.title: UK: PRESS DIGEST - British business press - May 1.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - British business press - May 1.

text.p: Prepared for Reuters by The Broadcast Monitoring Company
DAILY TELEGRAPH
-- HALIFAX DOCKS MEMBERS 520 MILLION POUNDS

The Halifax Building Society yesterday said more than 400,000 members had lost their entitlements to windfall shares. Children, the elderly and the disabled are likely to feature prominently among the losers. The society has been criticized as making its eligibility rules unnecessarily complicated, but insists it has applied the statutory requirements of the Building Society Act.
-- BAT HEDGES POSITION ON LIABILITIES COVER

BAT Industries has defied demands from major shareholder Neil Woodford of Perpetual to detail whether its general insurance policies could cover any tobacco liabilities in the USA. Mr Woodford had asked for comment on research from Schroders that indicated industry insurance for tobacco liabilities could stretch as far back as the 1930s.
-- BOOSEY & HAWKES UP FOR SALE AT 170 MILLION POUNDS

Boosey & Hawkes, the music publisher and instrument maker, has been put up for sale by the American family that controls 45 per cent of its shares. The Carl Fischer Inc-stake is owned by the Connor family. Its sale will automatically result in a bid for B&H under the Takeover Code. Shares jumped 70 to 867.5p at
the news.
THE TIMES
-- US GROWTH FIGURES CAUSE MARKET TURBULENCE

Trading was turbulent on the London and New York markets yesterday after new data showed that the US economy is growing at its fastest pace for nine years. First-quarter US GDP grew 5.6 percent, compared with 3.8 percent the previous quarter.
-- LABOUR'S LAW WOULD RING-FENCE THE CO-OP

The Labour party confirmed yesterday its intention, if elected, to bring forward a bill to protect the co-operative movement in the wake of a hostile bid by Andrew Regan's Galileo vehicle. Shadow economic secretary to the treasury Mike O'Brien confirmed the bill had already been drafted. Parliamentary support for the bill is likely to be strong.
-- GKN TO STRENGTHEN 'POWER MET' BUSINESS WITH US DEAL

GKN has moved to strengthen its powder metallurgy business by spending 352 million pounds stg to buy Sinter Metals of the United States. 'Powder met' is becoming the favoured metal components manufacturing method, and GKN said the deal would make it world leader in the area.
THE GUARDIAN
-- CAMPAIGNING SHAREHOLDERS ATTACK BAe ARMS SALES

British Aerospace ejected almost half the shareholders at its annual meeting in London yesterday after disruption by anti-arms protesters who had bought one share each. Protests focused on alleged use of BAe products by Indonesia in East Timor.
-- BOSSES BALK AT PROTEST TACTICS

Tim Melville-Ross, director-general of the Institute of Directors, yesterday called for laws to stop disruption of shareholders' meetings by pressure groups. He called for protestors to take a more discreet approach, and company directors to take an 'open and honest' approach in return.
-- INVESTORS IMPATIENT TO SEE GAS PRICE REPORT

Gas shareholders called for immediate publication of a Monopolies and Mergers Commission report on price controls for British Gas's GAS.L Transco pipeline business. The chief executive of BG, the British Gas demerged sector responsible for Transco, said the success of competition in the gas market could be threatened unless the MMC inquiry gave Transco stability.
THE INDEPENDENT
-- FORMULA ONE FLOTATION PLANS STALLED

Bernie Ecclestone has postponed plans to float his Formula One Grand Prix motor racing business in London and New York this summer, and is considering a private sale instead. Doubts also surround the 2.5-billion-pound-stg price tag originally put on the business.
-- BANKS ATTACK 'WHICH' REPORT

The British Building Association has mounted a pre-emptive strike against a report from the Consumers' Association, to be published today. The report in Which? magazine claims consumers will get a worse deal on mortgages and savings because of building society conversions and the need to pay dividends. The BBA said the report was from too narrow a perspective.
-- MURDOCH DIGITAL CONSORTIUM COULD BE WORTH 1.5 BILLION POUNDS

A report to be published today says British Digital Broadcasting, the consortium formed by BSkyB, Granada and Carlton to bid for the digital broadcasting licence, could be worth 1.5 billion pounds stg. The report says the largest share of profits will go to BSkyB, owned by Rupert Murdoch, if the consortium wins the licence.
